study.title: Acupuncture Modulates Resting State Hippocampal Functional Connectivity in Alzheimer Disease
study.study_design: single block experimental design, within-subject pre-post acupuncture fMRI, two-group comparison (AD patients vs healthy controls)
study.population: 14 patients with Alzheimer disease and 14 healthy elderly controls, all right-handed
study.inclusion_criteria: AD patients: complete physical and neurological examination, standard laboratory tests, extensive battery of neuropsychological assessments, fulfilled DSM-IV criteria for dementia and NINCDS-ADRDA criteria for possible or probable AD, CDR scores of 1 and 2. Healthy controls: no neurological or psychiatric disorders such as stroke, depression or epilepsy; no neurological deficiencies such as visual or hearing loss; no abnormal findings such as infarction or focal lesion in conventional brain MR imaging; no cognitive complaints; MMSE score of 28 or higher; CDR score of 0.
study.exclusion_criteria: Contraindications for MRI such as pacemakers, cardiac defibrillators, implanted material with electric or magnetic systems, vascular clips or mechanical heart valves, cochlear implants or claustrophobia. Patients with a history of stroke, psychiatric disease, drug abuse, severe hypertension, systematic diseases and intellectual disability.

interventions.procedure_label_exact: acupuncture stimulation on the Tai chong and He gu acupoints
acupoints_used_exact: Tai chong (Liv3, left and right feet)
He gu (LI4, left and right hands)
interventions.anatomical_location_exact: Tai chong: dorsum of left and right feet (first and second metatarsal cavity before integration); He gu: dorsum of left and right hands (between the first and second metacarpal and the midpoint of the second metacarpal radial side)
interventions.needle_size_exact: 0.30 mm in diameter and 25 mm long
interventions.needle_retention_exact: 3 minutes (during stimulation phase); needle withdrawn before post-acupuncture scan
interventions.session_duration_exact: 3 minutes acupuncture stimulation followed by 10 minutes post-acupuncture fMRI
interventions.participant_instructions_exact: remain still, keep their eyes closed and think of nothing in particular
interventions.treatment_rationale_given_exact: According to traditional Chinese medicine, AD belongs to the category of dementia. He gu is the original point of the large intestine channel of hand yangming (LI4), playing an important role in dispelling wind and analgesia and restoring consciousness. Taichong is the original point of the liver channel of foot jueyin (Liv3), which functions to relieve the depressed liver and subdue the endogenous wind and sedatives. He gu and Tai chong are collectively named the Si Guan (four gates) point. Combined use of these two acupoints can harmonize yin and yang, regulate qi and blood, finally improve the cognitive ability of AD patients.

neuroimaging_methods.sequence_exact: echo-planar imaging (EPI); also 3D T1-weighted magnetization-prepared rapid gradient echo (MPRAGE) sagittal images
neuroimaging_methods.voxel_size_exact: image matrix=64x64, slice number=33, thickness=3 mm, gap=1 mm (fMRI); image matrix=256x256, slice number=176, thickness=1 mm (MPRAGE)
neuroimaging_methods.scan_duration_exact: baseline resting state: 3 minutes; post-acupuncture resting state: 10 minutes
neuroimaging_methods.preprocessing_software_exact: SPM5 (http://www.fil.ion.ucl.ac.uk/spm); Resting-State fMRI Data Analysis Toolkit (http://resting-fmri.sourceforge.net)
neuroimaging_methods.smoothing_exact: Gaussian kernel of 4x4x4 mm3 full width at half maximum (FWHM)
neuroimaging_methods.motion_exclusion_exact: No participant had head motion of more than 1.5 mm displacement in any of the x, y, or z directions or 1.5° of any angular motion throughout the course of scan
neuroimaging_methods.global_signal_regression_exact: not_reported; white matter signal and CSF signal were regressed out
primary_neuroimaging_metrics: hippocampal functional connectivity (seed-based correlation, Fisher r-to-z transformed z values)
statistical_thresholds_exact: within-group one-sample t-test: P<0.01 and cluster size=405 mm3 (corrected threshold P<0.001 determined by Monte Carlo simulation, AlphaSim, FWHM=4 mm, within GM mask)
between-group two-sample t-test: P<0.01, single voxel threshold P<0.01 and cluster size 270 mm3 (AlphaSim, FWHM=4 mm with mask)
ROI independent-sample t-test: pre-acupuncture versus post-acupuncture
whole brain post vs pre acupuncture comparisons: P<0.01 uncorrected, extent threshold=20
neuroimaging_methods.multiple_comparison_correction_exact: Monte Carlo simulation using AlphaSim program; corrected threshold P<0.001 for within-group; P<0.01 for between-group differences

extraction_notes.note: Sensory/interoceptive responses during acupuncture (e.g., deqi, pain, numbness, heaviness) were not assessed or reported. No sensation rating scale was used.

There was no sham acupuncture condition. The authors acknowledge this as a study limitation: 'the current study would benefit from including a control state that could be compared with real-needle acupuncture, such as sham acupuncture.'
Expectancy, credibility, blinding success, and allocation guessing were not assessed or reported.

The paper describes an 'independent-sample t-test' for pre vs post acupuncture ROI comparisons within the same subjects; this appears to be a within-subject comparison mislabeled or using extracted mean z values per group rather than paired data. The exact statistical approach for these ROI comparisons is ambiguous.

The cluster size units in Tables 2, 3, and 4 are not explicitly labeled (mm3 vs voxels). The values appear to be small integers (e.g., 12, 13, 25, 56), most consistent with voxel counts at 3mm isotropic resolution, but this is not confirmed in the table headers.

Supplementary File S1 referenced in the paper contains additional results comparing acupuncture AD1 group vs non-acupuncture AD2 group (Table S1, S2, Figure S1, S2). These data could not be extracted as the supplement was not provided in the PDF.
The non-acupuncture AD2 group referenced in supplementary material is not described in the main methods section. Characteristics and sample size of this group are unknown from the main text.

The study does not clearly specify whether fMRI was acquired during the 3-minute baseline only or if there was also scanning during the acupuncture stimulation phase. From text: 'We first acquired baseline resting state data during the initial 3 minutes; we then performed acupuncture stimulation for the following 3 minutes. Last, we acquired fMRI data for another 10 minutes after the needle was withdrawn.' This implies fMRI was NOT acquired during stimulation, only before and after.

Table 2 notes 'P<0.01, uncorrected, extent threshold=10' which differs from the corrected Monte Carlo threshold described in methods (P<0.001 corrected, cluster size=405 mm3 for within-group; P<0.01 corrected, cluster size=270 mm3 for between-group). The threshold used in Table 2 appears to be uncorrected and more lenient.

The paper states 229 fMRI volumes remain after discarding the first 10. With TR=2000ms, this corresponds to approximately 7.6 minutes total acquired fMRI data. The breakdown between the 3-minute baseline and 10-minute post-acupuncture scans is not fully reconciled with the stated 229 volumes.

For Table 3 (AD post vs pre acupuncture whole brain), the two peaks listed for R MFG (BA 8 and BA 9) share the same cluster size of 25 but have different coordinates and Brodmann areas. It is unclear if they represent two separate clusters or two peaks within one cluster.

The paper uses the term 'increased connectivity' in multiple contexts that may reflect different statistical comparisons (within-group post vs pre, between-group AD vs NC). Each contrast was extracted separately as instructed, but readers should note these represent different analytical approaches.

No correlation between clinical outcomes (MMSE, AVLT) and neural connectivity changes was reported in the main text. The authors acknowledge this as a limitation and state they did not show cognitive performance correlations with functional connectivity changes induced by acupuncture treatments.
